statement.p:
Let's begin with the basis \bcal = \{\vvec_1,\vvec_2\} of \real^2 where
\vvec_1 = \twovec{3}{-2}, \vvec_2 = \twovec{2}{1} .
If the coordinates of \xvec in the basis \bcal are \coords{\xvec}{\bcal} = \twovec{-2}{4}, what is the vector \xvec?
If \xvec = \twovec{3}{5}, find the coordinates of \xvec in the basis \bcal; that is, find \coords{\xvec}{\bcal}.
Find a matrix A such that, for any vector \xvec, we have \xvec = A\coords{\xvec}{\bcal}. Explain why this matrix is invertible.
Using what you found in the previous part, find a matrix B such that, for any vector \xvec, we have \coords{\xvec}{\bcal} = B\xvec. What is the relationship between the two matrices A and B? Explain why this relationship holds.
Suppose we consider the standard basis \ecal = \{\evec_1,\evec_2\}. What is the relationship between \xvec and \coords{\xvec}{\ecal}?
Suppose we also consider the basis
\ccal = \left\{\twovec{1}{2}, \twovec{-2}{1}\right\} . Find a matrix C that converts coordinates in the basis \ccal into coordinates in the basis \bcal; that is,
\coords{\xvec}{\bcal} = C \coords{\xvec}{\ccal} . You may wish to think about converting coordinates from the basis \ccal into the standard coordinate system and then into the basis \bcal.

li.p: We solve the linear system c_1\vvec_1+c_2\vvec_2=\twovec{3}{5} to find \coords{\xvec}{\bcal}=\twovec{-1}{3}.
Since we have \xvec = A\coords{\xvec}{\bcal}, we also have A^{-1}\xvec = \coords{\xvec}{\bcal}.
